transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 10:30 AM PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (CTO, Seabreeze), Priya Raman (ML Eng), Omar Khalid (VP Product)

Summary (auto):
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, request params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retry behavior and idempotency, rate limits, and SDK demos. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a customer-facing assistant with strict latency targets (sub-300ms p50 for short queries) and SOC2/compliance needs. Agreed next steps: share pricing, security pack, sample benchmarks, and schedule a technical POC.

Topics: streaming responses, batching vs latency, retry/backoff, request params, KMS/encryption, SOC2 and SSO, pilot setup

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya with Redwood, AE. Diego, do you want to kick off on the demo side?
[00:12] Diego: Yeah, sure. Hi all, Diego Ruiz, solutions engineer. We'll do a quick hosted API walkthrough chat and text generation basics streaming, params, and how retries behave. I'll share my screen in a sec.
[00:22] Liam: Sounds good. We have about 40 minutes. We're mainly interested in latency tradeoffs and how retries won't cause double-charges or inconsistent state. Also SOC2 and data retention questions.
[00:32] Diego: Perfect, noted.

--- Screen share starts ---
[01:05] Diego: Ok, opening the Redwood Console demo page. This is the hosted API product view. On the left you can see model catalog, streaming controls, and on the right the playground for requests. Quick note names might appear slightly different from your internal docs, the auto trans sometimes says "Redwood Retime" instead of Redwood Runtime, so apologies up front for transcription.
[01:32] Priya: (laughs) that's fine.
[01:35] Diego: First demo: simple chat completion. I'm calling the /v1/chat/completions endpoint with messages that include system prompt, user query. We set temperature to 0.0 for deterministic answers and max_tokens to 120.
[01:48] Diego: [runs request] The response comes back as a stream; you'll see partial tokens arrive. Streaming is good for UX latency because tokens render as they arrive rather than waiting for the whole completion.
[02:05] Maya: From a product standpoint, customers often ask whether streaming counts as multiple billable events  it's a single API call, token billing is per-token regardless of streaming, so no double billing.
[02:18] Omar: Got it. For us, most queries are short  like 20 to 60 tokens. Our latency SLO is p50 250 300ms. Can you speak to cold-start vs warmed KV cache behavior?
[02:32] Diego: Sure. For short queries, the kernel selection and KV cache matter. On hosted, we do warming strategies and prefix caching where possible. Cold starts can be higher  maybe 50 100ms extra  depending on model and size. If you need deterministic p50 sub-300ms for small queries, we can recommend smaller model variants or reserved capacity (Dedicated).
[02:50] Priya: If we go hosted, how do retries work? Suppose we get a 5xx or a connection drop  will retrying repeat tokens or create duplicate side effects?
[03:02] Diego: Good question. For idempotency we recommend client-side idempotency keys for non-streaming operations that cause side-effects. For pure text generation, retries are safe but you may get different outputs unless you set deterministic params (temperature 0, top_p 0). Our SDK supports automatic exponential backoff for transient 5xx with configurable max attempts.
[03:20] Maya: Also important: streaming interruptions  the client may reconnect and we provide resume tokens for some model variants so you can continue the stream without repeating tokens. Not all older model variants support resume tokens; we'll send the compatibility matrix.

[03:40] Diego: I'm switching to parameters. We have temperature, top_p, max_tokens, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty. For safety and repeatability, set temperature to 0 or use top_p = 0. For creative outputs use higher temperature.
[03:58] Liam: Any guidance on tokenization and cost? We use mixed-language customer messages. Sometimes the token counts spike.
[04:08] Diego: Tokenization differences are real  UTF-8 multibyte characters and segmented languages change token counts. We provide a tokenizer helper in the SDK to estimate tokens pre-call, which helps guardrails and cost-estimates.

[04:25] Diego: Now I'll demo retries behavior in the SDK. (typing) Here is a Node example  fetch with retry and idempotency header. It will do up to 3 retries by default with jitter. If you want strict single-delivery semantics for calls that create records, we recommend a two-phase flow: generate offline and then commit once you validate response.
[04:48] Priya: Could you show streaming vs non-streaming throughput impact?
[04:52] Diego: Yes. Streaming reduces time-to-first-byte for the user but doesn't reduce per-token compute cost. For cost/throughput, batching multiple requests into a single GPU micro-batch improves unit economics; however, batching increases latency. On hosted we tune batching heuristics to balance both.
[05:14] Omar: What's the default rate limit for hosted accounts? We expect spikes during morning dispatch scheduling.
[05:20] Maya: Default soft limits depend on plan; typical starter tiers have 60 RPS global; we can raise that for pilot. For production with spikes, Dedicated with reserved capacity is recommended. We'll include the exact rate-limit table in the follow-up.

[05:40] Diego: Switching to the Console  observability. You can see request-level latency, per-token time, model version, and cost breakdown. There's a per-route dashboard and tracing hooks you can instrument. These help root-cause spikes  e.g., you can see if KV cache miss rate is causing p99 to jump.
[06:05] Liam: Can we run scheduled benchmarks? We need to compare two model variants for latency and quality.
[06:12] Diego: Yes  we provide benchmark scripts and a spreadsheet for you to run locally. I'll attach our benchmark template (link) and the sample results from similar logistics workloads.
[06:24] Priya: Also curious about security: data encryption at rest and in transit, KMS integration, and audit logs. We are SOC2 compliant and need SAML SSO.
[06:34] Maya: Redwood hosted is SOC2 Type II. We support customer-managed KMS for Dedicated; for hosted we use provider KMS but can provide audited keys rotation logs. SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs are available in enterprise plans. We'll share our security pack and attestation documents.
[06:55] Omar: What about data residency? Some of our customers are EU-only.
[07:00] Diego: Hosted supports region pinning for most EU regions; if you need strict on-prem or VPC-only, that's Private deployment. We'll include options and associated timelines.

[07:20] Diego: Quick demo of a streaming failure case  simulating dropped connection. (runs) You can see the client receives partial tokens. If the client reconnects and the model supports resume tokens, it resumes. Otherwise you can re-run with idempotency key to avoid duplicating downstream side-effects.
[07:45] Liam: Okay. For price modeling, can you provide examples of per-token vs per-request costs including streaming overheads?
[07:55] Maya: Yes, we'll send a pricing table. Streaming does not change per-token billing; we also show how batching and quantization (for Dedicated) reduce dollars per token. Redwood Optimize will suggest quantization steps and batching configs for your workload to get to target cost.

[08:15] Priya: For the POC, we want to test 100 RPS sustained with short prompt templates and measure p50/p95. Is hosted sufficient?
[08:25] Diego: For 100 RPS with tight p50s, hosted can handle it with a pilot quota increase, but Dedicated is more predictable. For the POC we can provision a pilot pool in Dedicated or run tests on hosted with a reserved box to simulate. We'll outline tradeoffs in the follow-up.

[08:45] Omar: Any gotchas about prompt templating and context windows? We use conversation history and sometimes pass 2  3k tokens of context.
[08:54] Diego: Conversation length matters. For long histories, we recommend KV caching or shortened embeddings + retrieval to keep token counts reasonable. Our Console shows token usage per request so you can iterate on template truncation.

[09:10] Maya: Quick note on quotas and billing: pilot accounts get temporary increases; the billing model is usage-based for hosted, and reserved for Dedicated with monthly/annual commits.

--- End demo screen share ---
[09:35] Liam: Great, this was helpful. A couple of clarifying questions: 1) For resume tokens and stream resumes, which models support it? 2) For the SDKs, any examples in Python?
[09:50] Diego: We'll send the compatibility matrix  generally newer Redwood-verified open models and our smaller variants support resume tokens. For Python, yes  we have examples in the repo and I'll paste a snippet in the follow-up message. The Node and Python SDKs both support streaming callbacks, retries, and token estimation.
[10:05] Priya: Also, can Diego run a short technical POC with our ML team next week to validate latency with our payloads?
[10:12] Diego: Absolutely, happy to.

[10:20] Maya: To recap  next steps: I'll email pricing and hosted vs dedicated comparison and SOC2/security pack. Diego will send benchmark spreadsheet, SDK snippets, and schedule the 45-min POC. Priya will confirm expected QPS and sample payloads.

[10:35] Liam: That works. Thanks Maya and Diego.
[10:38] Omar: Appreciate it.
[10:40] Diego: Thanks everyone  I'll follow up with links and the sheet.
[10:44] Maya: Bye all.
